title: Bay of Bengal Storm Likely to Hit Odisha-Andhra Coast as Cyclone Around October 28
excerpt: The IMD expects a low over the southeast Bay of Bengal to become a cyclonic storm by October 26, with red warnings for extremely heavy rain in coastal Odisha and north Andhra Pradesh.
body:
• A low-pressure area over the southeast Bay of Bengal is expected to intensify into a cyclonic storm by October 26 and make landfall on the Odisha-Andhra Pradesh coast around October 28, the IMD forecast indicates.
  • Red and orange rainfall warnings are in force: extremely heavy rain is likely in Odisha's coastal and southern districts and in north coastal Andhra Pradesh, with rough to very rough seas.
  • Fishermen have been advised not to venture into the sea, and those already out have been asked to return to the nearest harbour.
  • Families in the diaspora with homes and relatives in coastal Odisha and Andhra Pradesh should expect rail, road and power disruption around October 27-28 and check on district-level evacuation notices.

A low-pressure area over the southeast Bay of Bengal is likely to strengthen into a cyclonic storm over the next two days and cross the Odisha-Andhra Pradesh coast around October 28, bringing extremely heavy rain, strong winds and rough seas to the east coast, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said.

The system formed under the influence of an upper-air cyclonic circulation over the south Andaman Sea and is moving west-northwest, according to the IMD update reported by The Hindu. Forecasts indicate the low will become a depression and then a deep depression over the central and adjoining south Bay of Bengal by October 25-26, intensify into a cyclonic storm by October 26, and approach the coast between Odisha and Andhra Pradesh for landfall around October 28. The Indian Express, tracking the same IMD bulletins, reported landfall was likely between Machilipatnam and Kalingapatnam around Kakinada on the evening or night of October 28.

Warnings in force

The IMD has issued red and orange warnings across the threatened coast. Extremely heavy rainfall — more than 20 cm in 24 hours in the heaviest category — is likely over Rayalaseema on October 27-28 and over coastal and southern Odisha districts including Ganjam, Gajapati, Rayagada, Koraput, Malkangiri, Mayurbhanj, Balasore and Kendujhar around October 28-29, with heavy to very heavy rain also expected in West Bengal districts including Kolkata, Howrah, Hooghly and the Medinipurs and 24 Parganas. Squally winds strengthening to 50-60 km/h along the Odisha and north Andhra coasts are expected to build further as the storm nears, and sea conditions are forecast to turn rough to very rough from October 26.

"The system formed under the influence of an upper-air cyclonic circulation over the south Andaman Sea and is moving west-northwest, according to the IMD update reported by The Hindu ."

Fishermen have been advised not to venture into the sea along and off the Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal coasts, and those already at sea have been asked to return to the nearest harbour. Coastal residents have been told to stay alert for waterlogging, localised flooding and damage to kutcha houses and standing crops in low-lying areas.

A familiar October threat

October is peak season for Bay of Bengal cyclones, and Odisha's disaster machinery — built up after the 1999 super cyclone and tested by Phailin, Fani and Dana — typically begins evacuations from low-lying coastal villages once a landfall district is narrowed down. State governments in Odisha and Andhra Pradesh are expected to announce control rooms, school closures and evacuation orders as the track firms up over the next 48 hours.

What to watch

The IMD's next bulletins will fix the landfall district and the storm's peak wind speed, which decide the scale of evacuation. For readers abroad, the practical steps are concrete: confirm family travel plans around October 27-28, expect train and flight disruption into Bhubaneswar, Visakhapatnam and Vijayawada, and follow district administration notices rather than social-media forwards for evacuation information.
